title: India's GST Collections Just Surged 14% to ₹1.95 Lakh Crore — but Imports Are Doing the Heavy Lifting
excerpt: June's headline growth looks robust, but a 34.6% surge in import revenues is masking modest 6.5% domestic growth. The divergence tells a nuanced story about where India's economy actually stands.
body:
India's Goods and Services Tax collections rose 13.9% year-on-year to nearly ₹1.95 lakh crore in June 2026, according to provisional data released by the Finance Ministry on Wednesday. On the surface, it is a reassuring number — one that suggests the economy's consumption engine remains healthy. But a closer look at the composition reveals a story that is more complicated, and more consequential, than the headline suggests.

## The Import-Domestic Divide

The most striking feature of June's GST data is the widening gap between domestic and import-linked tax revenues. Gross collections from domestic transactions grew at a modest 6.5% to approximately ₹1.35 lakh crore. That is a solid number by most standards, but well below the 13.9% headline growth. The real engine behind the surge was import revenues, which jumped 34.6% to ₹60,038 crore — up from ₹44,600 crore in June 2025.

Import-linked IGST now accounts for roughly 31% of total gross collections, a share that has been steadily climbing. This reflects both a recovery in global trade volumes and, more importantly, the rebuilding of supply chains disrupted by the Iran-Strait of Hormuz crisis earlier this year. As Brent crude has crashed from its April war peak of $126 to around $72 per barrel, import volumes — particularly of crude oil, electronics, and industrial inputs — have recovered sharply.

## State-by-State: A Highly Uneven Picture

The state-wise data further complicates the narrative. Maharashtra, India's largest GST-contributing state, posted a 9% increase to ₹30,714 crore. Uttar Pradesh led major states with a 19% surge to ₹9,165 crore, followed by Assam at 17% and Punjab at 14%. Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, and Telangana each grew in the 10-12% range.



> **"As Brent crude has crashed from its April war peak of $126 to around $72 per barrel, import volumes — particularly of crude oil, electronics, and industrial inputs — have recovered sharply."**


But the picture is not uniformly bright. Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh each saw a 5% decline. Tamil Nadu's collections fell 2%. Jharkhand recorded a 16% drop. Most alarming, Uttarakhand's collections declined 21% and Himachal Pradesh reported a 26% fall — likely reflecting a combination of weak tourism demand and industrial softness.

## The Refund Puzzle

Total refunds during June rose 29.1% to ₹32,436 crore, a significant jump that reflects both improved processing timelines and the government's push to ease working capital pressures on manufacturers and exporters. After adjusting for refunds, net GST collections grew 11.2% to over ₹1.62 lakh crore.


![Finance Ministry — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cd/Government-Vedder-Highsmith-detail-1.jpeg)


The sharp rise in refunds is worth watching. While faster processing is a positive reform signal, sustained high refunds can also indicate that export-linked businesses are generating more input tax credits relative to domestic output — consistent with the import-heavy composition of the headline number.

## The Quarterly View

On a cumulative basis, total gross GST revenue for the first quarter of FY27 (April-June) reached ₹6.32 lakh crore, up 8.4% from ₹5.83 lakh crore in the corresponding period last year. Year-to-date domestic revenue grew just 2.8% to ₹4.54 lakh crore, while import revenue expanded 26.2% to ₹1.77 lakh crore.

The cumulative domestic growth rate of 2.8% is the figure that should give investors pause. It suggests that while India's formal economy is expanding, the pace of domestic consumption growth has decelerated meaningfully from the double-digit rates that characterized the post-pandemic recovery.

## What NRI Investors Should Watch

For NRI investors and India-watchers, the GST data offers a mixed but instructive read on the economy:

**The positives:** Import-led growth signals that India is restocking after the geopolitical disruption, oil prices are easing (reducing the current account deficit burden), and the formal economy continues to widen its base — the government's improved tax administration and compliance infrastructure are clearly working.

**The concerns:** The 6.5% domestic growth rate is a far cry from the robust consumption story that has underpinned India's premium valuation in global markets. The uneven state performance, with northern and central Indian states outpacing southern and eastern ones, hints at a consumption recovery that is not yet broad-based.

India's fiscal deficit for April-May stood at just 9.6% of the full-year target — well ahead of schedule and suggesting the government has room to spend. Whether that spending materialises in infrastructure or consumption-boosting measures will determine whether the second half of FY27 delivers the earnings acceleration that global fund managers are demanding before raising their India allocations.

The Nifty 50 rose 0.59% to 24,006 on Wednesday, with financials and auto stocks leading gains. Brent crude fell another 1% to $72. For now, the macro backdrop is improving. But the GST data's quiet message — that India's domestic demand engine is running on lower revs than the headline suggests — is one that careful investors should keep in their peripheral vision.
